newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council appeals again for end to Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council appeals again for end to Afghan war.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Wednesday called on Afghanistan's warring factions to work towards a negotiated peace although there were few signs the country's civil war was ending.
In a statement read at a public meeting, the council urged Afghan parties, in particular the dominant Taleban, to participate in "serious and honest" talks with U.N. mediators.
"The council strongly believes that a negotiated settlement is the only solution to the long-standing conflict in this country," the statement said.

The 15-member body was responding to a recent report by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan. He said that the Taleban, a purist Islamic movement that dominates two-thirds of the country, was determined to gain military control of all of Afghanistan and "establish their vision of an Islamic state."

The Taleban also wanted international recognition and a right to Afghanistan's seat at the United Nations, which they have little chance of securing in part because of their severe restrictions on work, education, dress and other measures against women and girls. U.N. humanitarian agencies have been in the forefront of denouncing these policies.

The council in its statement also demanded an immediate end to "the supply of arms and ammunition to all parties to the conflict." And it expressed deep concern at the discrimination against "women and other violations of human rights and of international humanitarian law in Afghanistan."

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia deny giving the Taleban arms. Russia and Iran, who back the opposition, have been accused of supplying weapons in the north. Annan in his report said both sides were "widely believed to be receiving material and financial support from external allies."
The Taleban has two principal opponents, the largely ethnic Tajik forces of military commander Ahmad Shah Masood and the ethnic Uzbek army of General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

During a two-day debate on the issue, Pakistan said it was time the council spoke directly to Taleban's envoys in New York, saying they were the "true voice of Afghanistan" and no peace could be negotiated without them.

The United States also has been accused of favouring the Taleban, in part because of Washington's support for the oil company Unocal competing for the right to build gas and oil pipelines from Turkmenistan, across Afghanistan, to Pakistan.
But American representative Edward Gnehm told the council earlier in the week that U.S. support for the Taleban was "disinformation."
"We do not support the Taleban or any other group," he said. "But neither do we put the blame on the Taleban for the ills of Afghanistan for which all parties are responsible."
